notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 5, drawn from the pages I was able to search and read.

---

## Psalm 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Title / Superscription

**"For the choirmaster, to be accompanied by flutes. A Psalm of David."**

- **Nehiloth** (translated "flutes") refers to wind instruments. Gill notes it comes from a root meaning "hollow," designating instruments such as the flute, cornet, pipe, trumpet, and hautboy. The Septuagint and Vulgate oddly render it "for that which obtained the inheritance," but the consensus is wind instruments. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/5.htm)
- JFB concisely says: "Upon Nehiloth — flutes or wind instruments." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/5.htm)
- Gray's Concise Commentary: "Nehiloth means flutes or wind instruments." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/psalms-5.html)
- Constable notes this is a morning prayer, contrasting with Psalm 4 as an evening psalm. It is an individual lament with elements of confidence, a community lament (vv. 11–12), and an imprecation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)

---

### v. 1: "Give ear to my words, O LORD; consider my groaning."

- **Gill:** "Words" denotes vocal prayer; "meditation" (or "groaning") denotes mental prayer — the silent musings of the heart. The root word also means "mourning" and can refer to inward groans, akin to the unutterable groanings of the Spirit (Rom. 8:26). God understands the language of a sigh. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/5.htm)
- **Expositor's Bible:** "Consider (or Understand) my meditation" — the brooding, silent thought is spread before God, who knows unspoken desires. The contrast between inward meditation and audible "cry" is intentional: meditations that do not pass into cries, and cries not preceded by meditation, are alike imperfect. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Using Hebrew parallelism, David repeats the same idea three times: "LORD, please listen to me." This reflects a deep longing for an actual audience with God, not merely the act of speaking words. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-5/)

---

### v. 2: "Attend to the sound of my cry, my King and my God, for to You I pray."

- **Guzik:** David prayed *to God*. Often we come to prayer so full of our requests or feelings that we never consciously focus on God. David's prayer time was focused on God Himself. He quotes R.A. Torrey: "Very much of so-called prayer, both public and private, is not unto God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-5/)
- **Expositor's Bible:** "My King" — if the singer is David, he thus recognises the delegated character of his own royalty. The intensely personal tone ("my King and my God") holds a plea in itself: the relationship brought about by God's love and accepted by faith is a ground for being heard. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)
- **Constable:** David viewed Yahweh as his King (who could deliver him) and as his God (who was his Father). VanGemeren calls "my God" the OT equivalent of "Abba Father." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)

---

### v. 3: "In the morning, O LORD, You hear my voice; at daybreak I lay my plea before You and wait in expectation."

- **Gill:** The morning is a proper time for prayer — to return thanks for sleep and preservation, to pray for protection through the day, for daily food, and for spiritual mercies. God should be served and sought first. The phrase "I will look up" expresses hope, expectation, faith, and confidence that an answer will come — like watching from a watchtower (cf. Hab. 2:1). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/5.htm)
- **Guzik:** Morning prayer sets the spiritual tone for the whole day. He cites Hudson Taylor (who woke at 2:00 a.m. for prayer) and Spurgeon ("An hour in the morning is worth two in the evening"). The word "direct" means "to order, to arrange" — the same word used for the priest laying out the morning sacrifice on the altar. Meyer adds: "It is manifestly a mistake to pray at haphazard." After prayer, we "look up" with expectancy. Spurgeon: "Let holy preparation link hands with patient expectation." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-5/)
- **Expositor's Bible:** The order of clauses is significant — God's hearing precedes the psalmist's praying. It is the order dictated by confidence: he who is sure God will hear will address himself to speak. The psalmist resolves to "order" his prayer, using the word for the priest's work of preparing the morning sacrifice. He also resolves to "keep watch" for the answer. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)
- **Gray's Concise Commentary:** "Look up" is rendered "keep watch" in the RV — the psalmist would keep watch on himself, that his life and conduct might be such as to insure the answer. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/psalms-5.html)

---

### v. 4: "For You are not a God who delights in wickedness; no evil can dwell with You."

- **Gill:** "Thou art not a God that hath pleasure in wickedness" argues from God's character — sin is contrary to His holy nature. God is so far from taking pleasure in sin that it is the abominable thing His righteous soul hates. "Neither shall evil dwell with thee" — the evil man who continues in wickedness has no communion with God now, nor shall he dwell with Him hereafter. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/5.htm)
- **Expositor's Bible:** The "for" would naturally have heralded a statement of why the psalmist expects to be welcomed. Instead it first regards God's holiness as *shutting out* the impure — a profoundly significant turn. "Thou art not a God that hath pleasure in wickedness" means more than "Thou hast not pleasure": it argues from the character of God and glances at foul pagan deities whose nostrils snuff up impurity as acceptable sacrifice. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)
- **Guzik:** As David drew closer to God, he became more aware of God's holiness and man's sinfulness. Boice: "If you are drawing close to God, you will become increasingly sensitive to sin." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-5/)
- **Constable:** David was aware that the One he petitioned was absolutely upright. Boastful and presumptuous people cannot count on standing before Him. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)

---

### v. 5: "The boastful cannot stand in Your presence; You hate all workers of iniquity."

- **Gill:** "The foolish" (KJV) — in Hebrew, the root word means "to praise," so it designates proud boasters, self-praisers, those elated with their own wisdom, strength, or righteousness who treat others with contempt. Their not "standing in God's sight" denotes God's abhorrence — like one who cannot bear to look upon someone. It also looks to the judgment day, when they will not be able to stand. "Thou hatest all workers of iniquity" — not all who have sin in them (for there are none without it), but those who make sin the business of their lives. God's hatred is His continued aversion to them and may include everlasting punishment. He is impartial: indignation and wrath come upon every soul that does evil. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/5.htm)
- **Constable:** Quoting the NET Bible note: "The LORD 'hates' the wicked in the sense that he despises their wicked character and deeds and actively opposes and judges them for their wickedness. See Psalm 11:5." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)
- **Expositor's Bible:** The first pair of designations are "the foolish" (or "arrogant") and "workers of iniquity" — a comprehensive pair. The psalmist's vocabulary is full of synonyms for sin, witnessing to the profound consciousness of it that law and ritual had evoked in devout hearts. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)

---

### v. 6: "You destroy those who tell lies; the LORD abhors the man of bloodshed and deceit."

- **Gill:** "Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing (lies)" — whether in religious matters (false doctrines, heresies — all who deny Christ are liars) or in common conversation. The destruction may be temporal (Gehazi's leprosy, Ananias and Sapphira's death) or eternal (all liars have their part in the lake of fire). "The man of blood and deceit" — one who thirsts after blood, who sheds innocent blood, and who flatters with a double heart. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/5.htm)
- **Expositor's Bible:** Only in this last pair are *specific* forms of evil mentioned — liars and men of blood and craft. "That specification surely witnesses to his own sufferings from such." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)
- **Constable:** God hates and destroys liars, deceivers, and murderers. C.S. Lewis remarked that the Jews cursed more bitterly than pagans "at least in part because they took right and wrong more seriously." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)

---

### v. 7: "But I will enter Your house by the abundance of Your loving devotion; in reverence I will bow down toward Your holy temple."

- **Gill:** "I will come into thy house" — the tabernacle; David was in exile from it but confident he would return. He would enter "in the multitude of thy mercy" — not relying on his own merits or righteousness, but on God's abundant mercy, grace, and goodness. The "temple" refers to the tabernacle. David may also have reference to the Messiah, whose human nature was typified by the tabernacle/temple, as the medium of divine worship. He would worship "in thy fear" — not slavish fear but reverence and godly fear, influenced by the multitude of mercy. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/5.htm)
- **Guzik:** David's confidence was not that he was righteous and others were sinners. His ground of confidence was the *mercy* of God. His worship wasn't based on feelings but on reverence for a righteous, merciful God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-5/)
- **Constable:** David did not claim a right to stand before God on the basis of his own righteousness. He believed God would be merciful because of the promises made to David and his house (2 Sam. 7). "Lovingkindness" (NASB) or "mercy" (NIV) means "loyal love" (Heb. *hesed*). The "house" and "temple" refer to the tabernacle David pitched for the ark in Jerusalem (2 Sam. 6:17). Rather than behaving arrogantly, David prostrated himself. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)
- **Expositor's Bible:** Very strikingly, David finds the ground of his right of entry not in his own innocence but in God's "multitude of mercy." "In the multitude of Thy mercy" and "in Thy fear" together set forth the conditions of approach. The word for "worship" means to prostrate oneself. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)

---

### v. 8: "Lead me, O LORD, in Your righteousness because of my enemies; make straight Your way before me."

- **Gill:** "Lead me, O Lord, in thy righteousness" — not in *mine*, but *thine*: the righteousness of God revealed in the Gospel, imputed by God and received by faith. David was sensible that the way of man is not in himself and he could not direct his own steps. "Because of mine enemies" — those who lie in wait, watching for his halting (as Jeremiah's enemies did). "Make thy way straight" — let it appear plain and manifest; remove obstructions (a probable reference to the enemies who lay in his way). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/5.htm)
- **Guzik:** This reflects David's constant reliance on God. He needed God to lead him and make the way straight. David walked the right way but was humble about it — he knew it was only God's power and work in him that kept him from the way of the wicked. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-5/)
- **Constable:** Essentially David asked for guidance in the righteous path God trod; he did not want to walk in the way of the wicked (vv. 4–6; cf. Psalm 1). Departure from it was a possibility because of the influence of the wicked. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)
- **JFB:** "Enemies — literally, 'watchers' (Ps. 27:11), hence special need of guidance." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/5.htm)
- **Expositor's Bible:** This is the only trace in the psalm of the presence of enemies. It is not so much that he fears falling into their hands as that he dreads lest, if left to himself, he may take some step that gives them occasion for malicious joy in his fall. "In Thy righteousness" probably means "because Thou art righteous" — His righteousness is manifested in leading those who seek His guidance. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)

---

### v. 9: "For not a word they speak can be trusted; destruction lies within them. Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit."

- **Gill:** "No faithfulness in their mouth" — no steadfastness, nothing that can be depended upon. "Their inward part is very wickedness" — the principle of all wickedness is within them; they are corrupt in their minds and conscience. "Their throat is an open sepulchre" — ready to devour men, as the grave swallows up corpses. "They flatter with their tongue" — they use smooth words to deceive. This passage is quoted by Paul in Romans 3:13 as part of his indictment of universal human depravity. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/5.htm)
- **Guzik:** David focused on what the wicked *say* as evidence of their wickedness (cf. Matt. 12:34 — "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks"). He quotes Spurgeon: "Always beware of people who flatter you, and especially when they tell you that they do not flatter you." Horne adds: a man's enemies, by obliging him to pray more fervently, often become his best friends. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-5/)
- **Expositor's Bible:** The sins here are those of speech. "Their inward part is destruction" (alternatively "a yawning gulf") — they plot inwardly the ruin of those they flatter. The throat is like an open sepulchre expanded in speech, and the falsely smoothed tongue is like a slippery approach to the descent. "Nothing stirs psalmists to deeper indignation than 'God's great gift of speech abused.'" (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)
- **Constable:** Their words lead to death; they are deceitful flatterers (cf. Rom. 3:13). They are untrustworthy in speech, determined to destroy rather than edify. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)

---

### v. 10: "Declare them guilty, O God; let them fall by their own devices. Drive them out for their many transgressions, for they have rebelled against You."

- **Guzik:** David prayed that the wicked would come to their deserved end. As rebels against God, they deserved the guilty sentence. This is an imprecatory prayer. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-5/)
- **Constable:** David asked God to hold the wicked guilty rather than let them escape consequences. He asked that they be snared in their own traps and thrust out — probably from positions of influence and ultimately from God's presence. This was legitimate because they had rebelled against the King of heaven. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)
- **Expositor's Bible:** The vindication for such prayers is that they are not expressions of personal enmity ("They have rebelled against Thee") and correspond to one side of the Divine character prominent in the OT era. Yet the commentary honestly adds: "But they do belong to that lower level; and to hesitate to admit their imperfection from the Christian point of view is to neglect the plain teaching of our Lord, who built His law of the kingdom on the declared relative imperfection of the ethics of the Old." It adds: "Let us be thankful that we dare not pray such prayers, but let us not forget that for the psalmist not to have prayed them would have indicated … that he had failed to learn the lesson of the law and was basely tolerant of baseness." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)

---

### v. 11: "But let all who take refuge in You rejoice; let them ever shout for joy. May You shelter them, that those who love Your name may rejoice in You."

- **Guzik:** The righteous aren't made righteous by their words; they are those who *trust* the LORD and *love* His name. Their righteousness is evident in their words — they rejoice, shout for joy, and are joyful. Spurgeon: "A touch of enthusiasm would be the salvation of many a man's religion. Some Christians are good enough people: they are like wax candles, but they are not lighted." Guzik notes this verse is a permit, a precept, a prayer, and a promise for joy. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-5/)
- **Expositor's Bible:** The order of designations is highly significant: first "those that trust in Thee," then "them that love Thy name," then "the righteous." "What is this sequence but an anticipation of the evangelical order? The root of all is trust, then love, then righteousness. Love follows trust. … Righteousness follows trust and love." The literal meaning of "put their trust" is "flee as to a refuge." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)
- **Constable:** Those who love God can count on His blessing and protection; they will respond with joyful singing. "Thy name" (found over 100 times in the Psalter) refers to God's character and attributes as revealed to human beings. This is the first of many references to singing in the Book of Psalms. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)

---

### v. 12: "For surely You, O LORD, bless the righteous; You surround them with the shield of Your favor."

- **Guzik:** This is the greatest blessing — the favor of God. A shield protects not just one area but is large and mobile enough to cover every area. This is how fully the favor of God, our standing in grace, protects us. He tells the story of Martin Luther, who when taunted about where he would find shelter if his patron deserted him, answered: "Under the shelter of heaven." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-5/)
- **Constable:** The whole psalm finds its focus in the faith expressed in verse 12. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)
- **Expositor's Bible:** Around the one who dwells in God's house and walks on God's path there is ever cast "the broad buckler of God's favour. He is safe from all evil on whom God looks with love, and he on whom God so looks is he whose heart dwells in God's house and whose feet travel on life's common way in cheerful godliness." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)

---

## Tradition-Specific Perspectives

Due to search and fetch limits, I was unable to retrieve dedicated pages from Ligonier (Reformed), Desiring God (Baptist), 1517.org (Lutheran), Seedbed (Methodist/Wesleyan), AG.org (Pentecostal), newadvent.org/catholic.com (Catholic), or OCA.org (Orthodox). From the material gathered, the following distinctives can be noted:

### Use of Psalm 5:9 in Reformed Theology (Total Depravity)
The Expositor's Bible Commentary and Gill both note that Paul quotes verse 9 in Romans 3:13 as part of his proof for universal human sinfulness — a key Reformed proof-text for total depravity. Gill specifically connects this to the doctrine that "there is none righteous, no, not one." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/5.htm); (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)

### Imprecatory Prayers (vv. 9–10) — Evangelical Discussion
The Expositor's Bible Commentary offers a nuanced take, acknowledging that these prayers belong to a "lower level" ethically than the New Testament, yet insisting that *not* praying them would have indicated a failure to take sin seriously. Constable notes C.S. Lewis's observation that the Jews "took right and wrong more seriously" than pagans, which explains the harshness. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm); (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)

### "The Foolish" (v. 5) — Variant Readings
Gill relates the Hebrew root (*halal*, "to praise") to "self-praisers" or "proud boasters," while the Expositor's Bible and most moderns prefer "arrogant." The LXX renders it "transgressors of the law." This is a rare point where translations differ, but no major doctrinal divide emerges from it. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/5.htm); (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm)

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship
The NET Bible note (cited by Constable) explains "hates" in verse 5 as "despises their wicked character and deeds and actively opposes and judges them for their wickedness" — a clarification aimed at readers troubled by the language of divine hatred. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)

### The "Temple" and Authorship Question
The Expositor's Bible Commentary addresses the critical question of whether "temple" (v. 7) rules out Davidic authorship (since Solomon's temple was not yet built). It notes that the same Hebrew word (*heykal*, "palace") is applied to the house of God at Shiloh in 1 Sam. 1:9 and 3:3, and can refer to any structure where God dwelt, even a tent. Thus it "cannot be urged as fatal to the correctness of the superscription," though it "does create a certain presumption against it." Constable likewise identifies it as the tabernacle David pitched for the ark in Jerusalem (2 Sam. 6:17). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/5.htm); (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-5.html)

---

## What I Could Not Find
- Dedicated commentary from specifically **Baptist** (Spurgeon's Treasury of David, Desiring God), **Methodist/Wesleyan** (Seedbed), **Lutheran** (LCMS, 1517.org), **Pentecostal** (AG.org, Sam Storms), **Catholic** (newadvent.org, catholic.com), or **Orthodox** (oca.org) sources. These would need additional searches and page reads beyond the limits reached.
- Modern debated teachings (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace readings of Psalm 5) — none of the pages retrieved addressed these.
